catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-rodrig:
Alonso Rodriguez was a Spanish Jesuit, born at Valladolid in 1526, dead at Seville in 1616. He entered the Society of Jesus at twenty and taught moral theology twelve years at Monterey College. He then served twelve years as master of novices, seventeen as rector, eleven as spiritual father at Cordova. As master of novices he oversaw the celebrated theologian Francisco Suárez. His characteristics in office were care and diligence.

The book he collected from his exhortations, published at his superiors' request, was meant for his brethren but also for other religious and laymen. Of set purpose it avoids lofty mysticism and abstruse speculation, offering practical instructions on the perfect Christian life, in cloister or world. It became popular at once and remains much used. More than twenty-five editions of the Spanish original appeared, besides extracts. Over sixty French editions in seven translations appeared, twenty Italian, ten German, eight Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-coello:
Alonzo Coello Sánchez, born at Benifayó in 1513 or 1515, dead at Madrid in 1590, bears a Portuguese name, likely his mother's. Philip II called him his Portuguese Titian for his close connexion with Portugal. Though nothing places Sánchez in Italy, he copied Titian under Antonio Mor, his great master. In 1552 he accompanied Mor to Lisbon to paint Portuguese portraits for Charles V.

One of the earliest Spanish court portrait-painters, he grew rich on great demand. He painted Gregory XIII, Sixtus V, Spanish grandees, Cardinal Farnese, and the Dukes of Florence and Savoy. He worked at the Escorial and painted Madrid's triumphal arch for Anne of Austria's entry, wife of Philip II. His most notable portrait may be St. Ignatius Loyola, from casts taken twenty-nine years before. His greatest was his friend Father Sigüenza, engraved by Selma. His colouring resembles Titian's; his portraits are powerful, lifelike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-sanche:
Alonzo Sánchez, born at Mondéjar in 1547, died at Alcalá in 1593. He entered the Society of Jesus at Alcalá in 1565, was rector of Navalcarnero college, and in 1579 went to Mexico as seminary rector. In 1581 he sailed for the Philippines with Bishop Salazar. Sánchez, Sedeño, and a lay brother led the first Jesuits into the islands. The bishop made Sánchez counsellor and synod acts writer.

Chosen by officials, merchants, and leading citizens, Sánchez went to Madrid in 1586 as the colony's representative. His mission moved Philip II to retain the islands against advisors urging abandonment. From Madrid he went to Rome, where Sixtus V granted privileges for the Philippine Church. Gregory XIV's brief of June 1591 praised his labours, calling him a defender of the Holy See's authority and rights. Clement VIII granted favours to the islands' bishop and clergy on his request.

george-walker-at-suez:
Anthony Trollope cast a plain London businessman as hero of George Walker at Suez, a short tale from Tales of All Countries. George Walker of Friday Street narrates his own adventure with honesty. Sent to Cairo for a sore throat, he suspects his partners wanted him out of the firm. Lonely hotel days in Egypt humble a man who craved homage.

Suez itself disgusts him: sand, heat, no water, and a cavernous hotel stripped of comforts. One day of that dull week, though, lends a halo to the trip in his memory. Passengers bound for Australia sweep through Cairo and Suez in flocks between steamers and trains. Among strangers, Walker tastes the respect and notice that London never gave him. Trollope keeps the scale tiny and the irony gentle. Readers who enjoy quiet character comedy, where a nobody's pride takes a holiday, will savor this brief Egyptian episode.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AlvarezLuisDr_D: Dr. Luis Alvarez was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist who turned his science on the Kennedy assassination, testing what the Zapruder film and the physics of the shots could prove. This file holds the government material filed under his name in the assassination records. Alvarez's experiments, including his famous work on the head shot's movement, made him the best-known scientist in the case. The file is kept as issued, part of the record of science entering the assassination debate.
